**BPMN standard convergence.** Four of the five flow nodes this engine used to reject now load, and
the rejected list is down to **one** — `<event>`, which is `abstract="true"` in the BPMN 2.0 XSD
and so cannot be implemented by anyone.

**Purely additive.** No element that loaded before loads differently, no package format or
persistence schema moved, and the `q:` surface did not change. A package sealed by 0.3.0 deploys
unchanged. See [Upgrading](#upgrading) — there is nothing to do.

## The rule, because the list is a consequence of it

Where BPMN 2.0 already spells something the engine does, **accept the standard spelling and map it
onto existing behaviour**. Keep `q:` for what BPMN cannot model, and keep it visibly an extension.

Two locally-reasonable forces had pushed the engine away from the standard. Fail-closed is the house
style, and it is right when the alternative is silence — but wrong for elements the engine could
execute trivially, where it rejected conformant models and bought nothing. And `q:` was the path of
least resistance: ours, expressive, easier than a frozen spec. Each time something went there that
BPMN already spells, the surface drifted from what a practitioner knows, and a reader could no
longer tell which parts are the standard and which are ours.

## What now loads

| Element | Maps to | What it used to say |
|---|---|---|
| `<task>` | a pass-through, as `<manualTask>` already is | "an abstract task has no behaviour" — true, and `<manualTask>` has none either |
| `<implicitThrowEvent>` | an intermediate throw | the spec distinguishes how it is *reached*, not what it does |
| `<receiveTask>` | a wait-capable **activity** | "use an intermediateCatchEvent" — behaviourally right, but an event cannot host a boundary |
| `<eventBasedGateway>` | a race over its arms | "racing wait states are not modelled" |
| non-interrupting timer boundary | host keeps waiting; a token leaves via the boundary | "only INTERRUPTING timer boundaries are supported" |
| `<timeCycle>` on such a boundary | recurring escalation | "a token parks exactly once" — true of a catch, not of this |
| `<property>`, `<dataObject>`, `itemDefinition` | declared variables | nothing: they were read not at all |

### `<receiveTask>` — why, when a catch event already parks

It parks identically. The point is that it is an **activity**, so a boundary event can attach —
which is how BPMN says *"wait for this message, or time out"*:

```xml
<bpmn:receiveTask id="AwaitSettlement">
  <bpmn:extensionElements><q:source channel="responses"/></bpmn:extensionElements>
</bpmn:receiveTask>
<bpmn:boundaryEvent id="Timeout" attachedToRef="AwaitSettlement">
  <bpmn:timerEventDefinition><bpmn:timeDuration>PT30M</bpmn:timeDuration></bpmn:timerEventDefinition>
</bpmn:boundaryEvent>
```

An event cannot host a boundary, so a catch event could never express that shape. The only previous
route was a channel-call service task — which needs a request leg a receive task does not have.

### `<eventBasedGateway>` — a race, resolved atomically

The gateway does **not** park. It arms its *targets*, which are already wait states, so one token
enters and one leaves. The first arm to fire wins, and the losing arms are retired **in the same
transaction that advances the winner** — because a losing timer row left pending would fire later
and send a second token through a gateway that had already resolved.

Three refusals at load, each because the alternative is silent wrongness:

- **An arm that does not park.** BPMN requires catch events or receive tasks. An arm that resolves
  instantly makes every other arm unreachable.
- **Fewer than two arms.** A one-armed race is not a race; park on the catch event directly.
- **`eventGatewayType="Parallel"` and `@instantiate="true"`.** `Parallel` is meaningful only when
  instantiating, and silently treating it as `Exclusive` would invert "wait for all" into "wait for
  one".

### Recurring escalation

```xml
<bpmn:boundaryEvent id="Nag" attachedToRef="Approve" cancelActivity="false">
  <bpmn:timerEventDefinition><bpmn:timeCycle>R/PT2H</bpmn:timeCycle></bpmn:timerEventDefinition>
</bpmn:boundaryEvent>
```

Every two hours while `Approve` is still parked, a token goes down the boundary's path and the host
keeps waiting. No new timer logic: this reuses the cycle engine the deployment schedule poller
already uses, so a boundary cycle and a timer-start cycle share one catch-up policy — each claim
fires exactly once, and slots that elapsed while the engine was down are **skipped rather than
replayed as a burst**.

### BPMN's data vocabulary

`<property>`, and `<dataObject>`/`<dataObjectReference>` when a data association names them, now
declare variables, with the type from `itemDefinition` where resolvable. Before this the loader read
**none** of it, so a model authored in a BPMN tool lost its data declarations silently — nothing was
even rejected.

`<q:variables>` remains authoritative, because four of its six attributes have no BPMN equivalent:
`transient` (never persisted), `sensitive` (persisted but redacted in logs, audit and diagnostics),
`subjectKey` (blind-indexed so the instances holding a data subject can be enumerated), and `source`
(a feed-off from a channel's intake). BPMN is a notation, not an execution-state specification: it
models neither persistence nor redaction nor data-subject indexing, and should not.

A name declared both ways is won by `<q:variable>`, type included — an untyped `<q:variable>` is a
deliberate `Any`, not an omission to back-fill from a different spelling, and filling it would make
the effective type depend on which file the author edited. The loser is reported, not swallowed:
`SUTRA.CONFIG.BPMN.VARIABLE_SPELLING_CONFLICT`.

## Limitations, stated rather than discovered

- **A bounded `R<n>` cycle on a boundary is rejected.** The remaining budget would have to survive
  the host activity's park, which means durable per-instance state and a snapshot format change. Use
  `R/<interval>` and end the recurrence by completing the host.
- **`<event>` will never be implemented.** `tEvent` is abstract — it is the substitution-group head,
  and no conformant document can use it as a flow node. This is the one row left in the rejected
  table, and it is a statement about the spec rather than about this engine.
- **An instantiating `<receiveTask>` / `<eventBasedGateway>` is rejected**, with `<startEvent>`
  named as the alternative: process instantiation needs the intake-selection surface a start event
  has.

## Upgrading

**Nothing to do.** Two new `sutra lint` **warnings** may appear on existing models, neither
blocking: `SUTRA.CONFIG.BPMN.UNTYPED_TASK` on an untyped `<task>`, and
`SUTRA.CONFIG.BPMN.VARIABLE_SPELLING_CONFLICT` where a variable is declared both ways.

## Security

`tokio` 1.53.1 → 1.54.1 for `RUSTSEC-2026-0386` (`AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate
I/O safety), published after 0.3.0.

Three residual advisories remain triaged rather than fixed: `rustls` 0.21 and `rustls-webpki` 0.101
reach the tree only through `tiberius 0.12.3 → tokio-rustls 0.24`, which is the latest release and
pins them. Both modern lines already carry the fixes. The entries are time-boxed with their
justification in `rust/.cargo/audit.toml` and `rust/deny.toml`.
